blocks.content: Imagine a bank account shared by a husband and wife. The account balance is ₹10,000. At the exact same moment, both open their banking app and try to transfer ₹8,000. If the bank's system does not properly coordinate these operations, both transactions may read the same balance before either update is recorded.
As a result, both transfers succeed even though the account only had enough money for one. The balance becomes incorrect, money appears to vanish, and the system enters an invalid state.

The problem isn't that either transaction was wrong in isolation the problem is that they happened simultaneously and interfered with each other. Software systems face the same challenge whenever multiple threads access and modify shared data at the same time.
1. What is Thread Safety
Code is thread-safe when it behaves correctly no matter how many threads call it simultaneously and no matter how the operating system happens to interleave their execution.

The danger isn't theoretical it's that counter++ is not one operation at the machine level. It's read, then add one, then write back. If two threads interleave those three steps, one increment vanishes, silently, with no error and no exception.

This lesson covers: the anatomy of a race condition, the live demonstration below, locks and atomics as the fix, the readers-writer lock optimization, deadlock, and the mistakes that produce thread-safety bugs which only show up under production load.
Without a Lock
When both threads access the shared counter at the same time, neither thread knows what the other is doing. Suppose the counter value is 100. Thread 1 reads 100 and prepares to increment it to 101.
Before it can write the value back, Thread 2 also reads 100 and prepares to increment it to 101. Both threads eventually write 101 to memory.

Although two increments were performed, the counter increased only once. One update was silently overwritten by the other, causing the final result to be lower than expected. This is known as a race condition.
With a Lock

A lock ensures that only one thread can access the critical section at a time. When Thread 1 acquires the lock, Thread 2 is forced to wait. Thread 1 reads the counter, increments it, writes the updated value back, and then releases the lock.

Only after the lock is released can Thread 2 enter the critical section and perform its increment. Since the operations happen one after another rather than simultaneously, no updates are lost and the final counter value is always correct.

blocks.content: 2. What Lock and Unlock Actually Do
blocks.text: 2. What Lock and Unlock Actually Do

blocks.content: Locking is the act of reserving a shared resource so that only one thread can modify it at a time. Unlocking releases that reservation and allows another waiting thread to proceed.
Together, lock and unlock transform a non-deterministic operation into a predictable one by preventing multiple threads from modifying shared state simultaneously.
The unsafe version allows both threads to interfere with each other, while the safe version uses a lock to guarantee that every increment is counted exactly once.
3. Anatomy of the race
blocks.text: 3. Anatomy of the race

blocks.content: The bug exists because counter++ is really three CPU-level steps: read the current value into a register, increment the register, write the register back to memory.
If thread A reads 41, then thread B also reads 41 before A writes back, both threads compute 42 and both write 42. One increment is lost the counter should be 43.
Both threads are trying to increment the same counter, which initially has a value of 41.

Thread A reads 41 and calculates 42, but before it writes the result back, Thread B also reads the same value 41 and calculates 42. Since memory still contains 41 during this time, both threads think they are working with the latest value.
Thread A writes 42 to memory. Later, Thread B also writes 42, overwriting the value written by Thread A.

As a result, the counter ends at 42 instead of 43. Even though two increments were performed, only one increment is reflected in the final result. This lost update is a classic race condition caused by multiple threads modifying shared data without synchronization.
4. The fix: mutual exclusion

A lock (mutex) guarantees that only one thread can execute the critical section the read-modify-write sequence at a time. Any other thread that tries to enter while the lock is held simply waits. This serializes the operation without serializing the entire program.

The problem occurs because multiple threads are allowed to access and modify the shared counter at the same time. The solution is mutual exclusion, which means ensuring that only one thread can enter the critical section at any given moment.
When a thread wants to update the counter, it first acquires a lock. While that lock is held, all other threads must wait.

The thread reads the current value, performs the increment, writes the updated value back to memory, and then releases the lock. Only after the lock is released can another thread enter and perform its update.

By forcing threads to access shared data one at a time, mutual exclusion prevents race conditions and guarantees that every increment is counted correctly. Instead of competing with each other, the threads take turns, ensuring the final result is always correct and predictable.

Note Python's case specifically: even with the GIL,count += 1is not guaranteed atomic, because it compiles to multiple bytecode instructions and the GIL can switch threads between any two of them. 

The GIL prevents true parallel execution of Python bytecode, but it does not prevent interleaving the lock is still required.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 5. A lighter alternative: atomics

For simple operations like incrementing a counter, a full mutex is heavier than necessary. Atomic types provide hardware-level guaranteed atomicity for single operations no lock acquisition overhead, no possibility of blocking.

blocks.content: 6. Readers-Writer lock

A plain mutex serializes everyone, even when ten threads only want to read a value that never changes during their visit. A readers-writer lock allows any number of concurrent readers, but gives exclusive access to a single writer when one needs to modify the data.
This is the right tool when reads vastly outnumber writes a configuration cache, for example.
So, Readers-Writer Lock is an optimization used when a shared resource is read frequently but updated rarely.
Instead of allowing only one thread at a time, it permits multiple readers to access the data simultaneously because reading does not modify the state.
In the diagram, Reader A, Reader B, and Reader C are all reading the same configuration cache at the same time.
Since none of them are changing the data, they can safely proceed concurrently without blocking each other, improving throughput and reducing waiting time.
When a writer needs to update the cache, the situation changes. The writer must obtain exclusive access to the resource.
During the update, no readers are allowed to read the cache, and no other writers can modify it. This guarantees that readers never see partially updated data and that the cache remains consistent.
In short, a Readers-Writer Lock allows many readers at the same time, but when a write operation occurs, the writer gets exclusive access until the update is complete.
This makes it ideal for systems such as configuration caches, product catalogs, routing tables, and reference data where reads greatly outnumber writes.
7. Deadlock ( the cost of locking wrong )
blocks.text: 7. Deadlock ( the cost of locking wrong )

blocks.content: Locks fix races but introduce a new failure mode: two threads each hold a lock the other needs, and neither will ever release. The classic scenario is two threads acquiring the same two locks in opposite order.
This diagram shows a deadlock, a situation where two threads are waiting for each other forever.
Thread A has already acquired Lock 1 and now wants Lock 2 to continue its work. At the same time, Thread B has already acquired Lock 2 and wants Lock 1 to continue.

Thread A cannot proceed until Thread B releases Lock 2, and Thread B cannot proceed until Thread A releases Lock 1. Since both threads are waiting for a lock that the other thread is holding, neither can make progress.

As a result, both threads become permanently blocked, the application stops making progress, and the system enters a deadlock state. This is often called a circular wait, where each thread is waiting for a resource held by another thread in the cycle.

["Always acquire locks in a consistent global order.If every thread acquires Lock 1 before Lock 2, the circular wait shown above becomes structurally impossible one thread will always get Lock 1 first and proceed.
","Keep critical sections small.Acquire the lock right before the shared data access, release it right after. Don't do I/O, logging, or other slow work while holding a lock.
","Never call back into unknown code while holding a lock.A callback or event listener might try to acquire the same lock, or a different lock in conflicting order, causing deadlock from code you don't control.
","Use a timeout on lock acquisition where deadlock would be catastrophic.tryLock(timeout)in Java or a timedstd::unique_lockin C++ lets the program detect and recover from a stuck lock rather than hanging forever.
"]

blocks.content: 8. Immutability
The simplest way to make data thread-safe is to make it impossible to mutate.

An immutable object can be freely shared and read by any number of threads with zero synchronization, because there is no write to race against. This is why functional-style code with immutable data structures is naturally easier to parallelize.
This diagram shows one of the simplest ways to achieve thread safety: immutability.

Immutable data means that once an object is created, its state can never be changed. Since no thread can modify the data, multiple threads can safely read it at the same time without using locks or synchronization.

In the diagram, Thread A, Thread B, and Thread C are all reading the same immutable object. Because the data never changes, there is no risk of one thread seeing a partially updated value or overwriting another thread's work. Every thread sees exactly the same state.

As a result, all threads can access the data concurrently without race conditions, deadlocks, or synchronization overhead. This makes immutable objects naturally thread-safe and often the easiest way to share data between threads safely.
9. Common mistakes

Mistake 1: checking then acting without holding the lock across both stepsCheckingif (map.containsKey(key))and then callingmap.get(key)as two separate locked operations leaves a window where another thread can remove the key between the check and the get. The check-then-act sequence must happen under a single lock acquisition, not two.

Mistake 2: synchronizing the wrong object Locking on a new object created inside the method, or on a boxed value that gets replaced, provides zero protection every thread locks a different object and none of them actually exclude each other. The lock must be a single shared instance that every thread agrees to coordinate on.

Mistake 3: assuming a "thread-safe" collection makes the whole operation safe A thread-safe map guarantees each individualputorgetis atomic, but composing two calls read a value, compute something, write it back is still a race unless that compound operation is wrapped in its own lock or uses an atomic compare-and-swap method.

Mistake 4: holding a lock during a network call or I/O Locking a shared resource, then making an HTTP call before releasing it, turns a fast in-memory operation into a slow one that blocks every other thread for however long the network takes under load this can serialize an entire service down to one request at a time.

Mistake 5: inconsistent lock ordering across the codebase One code path locks A then B; another locks B then A. Both are individually correct, but together they create exactly the circular-wait deadlock shown above, and it may only manifest under specific timing that production traffic eventually hits.
10. Quick reference

["Race condition Two threads interleave a non-atomic read-modify-write, silently losing an update. No exception, no crash just a wrong number.
","Mutex / lock Serializes access to a critical section. Correct but adds contention every thread waits its turn.
","Atomic Hardware-guaranteed single-operation safety. Lighter than a lock, but only covers one operation at a time.
","Readers-writer lock Many concurrent readers, one exclusive writer. Right for read-heavy shared state like caches.
","Deadlock Circular wait on locks held in opposite order. Fix: consistent global lock ordering.
","Immutability No mutation, no race possible. The simplest and most robust thread-safety strategy when it fits the design."]
